title: Religious Experience: William James and Beyond
welcome_lead: Wander with William James through saints' diaries, conversion stories and mystical reports as he asks what religious experience tells us about reality.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on religious experience: William James's four marks, Otto, Swinburne's principles, and critiques.

walkthroughs.body_html: William James's The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), the Gifford Lectures, takes a pragmatic and empirical approach. He famously brackets institutional religion to focus on personal experience. Mystical experiences share four marks: ineffability (cannot be fully communicated), noetic quality (yields knowledge), transiency (rarely lasts long), and passivity (the self feels grasped by something other).

Rudolf Otto, in Das Heilige (1917, translated as The Idea of the Holy), coins 'numinous' from numen. The holy is encountered as mysterium tremendum et fascinans: a mystery that both terrifies and attracts. This is, for Otto, a category sui generis, not reducible to ethics or aesthetics.

Richard Swinburne, in The Existence of God (1979), argues that religious experience is good probabilistic evidence for God. By the Principle of Credulity, take experience at face value unless defeated. By the Principle of Testimony, believe others unless they are unreliable. Critics like Anthony Flew counter that we have strong defeaters (varied and conflicting reports) and Freudian explanations to consider.
